title: JavaScript Runtime: Execution Contexts, Stack, Heap, and Garbage Collection
description: Trace execution contexts and closures, reason about reachability, and diagnose stack overflow and memory-retention bugs.
learningOutcomes: Explain execution context and its creation/execution model at a useful conceptual level.
Trace nested calls with the call stack and identify uncontrolled recursion.
Distinguish value identity, object references, and reachability.
Explain garbage collection using reachability/mark-and-sweep as a mental model.
Diagnose closure retention and unintended memory growth with evidence.
Predict how assignment, shallow copies, and structured cloning affect nested object identity.
Investigate memory growth with repeatable heap snapshots, retaining paths, and allocation profiling.
Design a memoization key that captures semantic inputs and explain cache lifetime and invalidation.
Implement async memoization with in-flight Promise sharing, TTL expiry, rejected-entry eviction and safe invalidation.

blocks.text: What runtime internals help you debug?

JavaScript source is executed inside a runtime that manages lexical environments, active function calls, object memory, queued jobs and host APIs. The ECMAScript specification defines language behavior; engines such as V8 choose implementation strategies. Treat stack/heap diagrams as useful models, not an exact map of physical machine memory or a guarantee about one engine's optimization.

blocks.title: Separate the questions
blocks.text: Execution context: what environment is executing now? Call stack: which calls are active and in what order? Heap/reachability: which allocated objects remain reachable? Event loop/host queues: when can queued work run after the current JavaScript stack finishes? These questions connect, but they are not interchangeable.

steps.title: Calling outer adds an active call
steps.explanation: The runtime establishes the function's execution context and evaluates its statements. The local label is a binding in this invocation's lexical environment.

steps.title: The nested call becomes the active top frame
steps.explanation: inner runs before outer continues. Its local label shadows any outer variable of the same name, so the log prints inner.

steps.title: Returning restores the caller
steps.explanation: When inner returns, its frame is removed and execution continues after inner() in outer. The stack follows last-in, first-out order.

blocks.text: Every nested function call needs execution bookkeeping. Recursion is valid when progress and a base case are guaranteed; a cycle that keeps calling without approaching a base case can exhaust the engine's stack and throw a RangeError such as 'Maximum call stack size exceeded'. Use the stack trace to find the repeating call path instead of increasing a stack limit as the first fix.
Heap objects, reachability, and garbage collection

Objects and closures may remain allocated while they are reachable from roots such as active stacks, global bindings or host-held references. A common garbage-collection model is mark-and-sweep: identify reachable objects, then reclaim unreachable ones. Real engines use generational, incremental and concurrent strategies, so collection timing is not predictable and memory is not necessarily returned to the operating system immediately.
Value identity, references, and copy depth

A variable binding holds a value. When that value is an object, assigning it to another binding copies the reference value, so both bindings can reach the same object. A shallow copy creates a new outer object but reuses nested object and array references. This is language-level behavior; stack/heap placement is an implementation detail and is not specified by JavaScript.

steps.title: Assignment copies an object reference
steps.explanation: alias and original refer to one object. The spread makes a different outer object, but the nested profile and tags values are still shared.

steps.title: Nested writes reveal the shared references
steps.explanation: The profile mutation through alias is visible through original and shallow. Pushing through shallow.tags also changes original.tags because that array was not copied.

steps.title: A structured clone separates supported data
steps.explanation: The clone captures the nested values as they were at that moment. Later edits to original do not alter independent. structuredClone supports many structured-cloneable values, not every value or every custom behavior; choose an explicit domain-specific copy when needed.

blocks.prompt: After `const shallow = { ...original }`, which statement is true if `original.profile` is an object?

options.text: The spread recursively clones every nested value.
options.feedback: Object spread is shallow: nested object references are copied as values, not recursively cloned.

options.text: `shallow` is a new outer object, while `shallow.profile` initially refers to the same nested object.
options.feedback: The outer identity differs, but the nested reference is shared until you explicitly copy that nested structure.

options.text: JavaScript guarantees that `original` is physically stored on the stack.
options.feedback: The language specifies observable behavior, not a universal physical stack/heap layout for each binding or object.

options.text: Changing `shallow.profile` can never affect anything reachable from `original`.
options.feedback: Because the nested object is shared, mutating one of its properties is visible through either path.

blocks.explanation: Predict identity at each nesting level. A shallow copy separates only the outer container.

blocks.title: Diagrams are models, not memory maps
blocks.text: JavaScript does not promise that primitives live on a physical stack, objects have visible numeric addresses, strings use a particular intern pool, or V8 always uses a named optimization pipeline. Engine versions and optimizations change. Use stack/heap pictures to reason about calls and reachability, and use runtime documentation plus measurements for engine-specific questions.

A high reading after one action is not enough to prove a leak: caches, delayed collection, warm-up, and temporary allocations can all raise memory. Reproduce the same action several times, take comparable heap snapshots, compare retained objects, and inspect retaining paths back to roots. Check that cleanup actually ran for listeners, timers, subscriptions, detached DOM, and long-lived collections. Allocation sampling or a timeline can show when objects are created; interpret it alongside the user-visible lifecycle and engine documentation.

In Chrome DevTools, use Memory → Heap snapshot to inspect retained objects and retaining paths, and compare snapshots after equivalent actions and cleanup. Use Allocation instrumentation on timeline or sampling to investigate when growth occurs. A snapshot is evidence to interpret, not an automatic leak verdict.
Memoization is a cache contract, not a universal speed switch

Memoization stores a result and reuses it when a later call has the same semantic inputs. It suits deterministic calculations where repeated work is measurably expensive. The key must include every input that can change the result; use an explicit key selector rather than assuming `JSON.stringify(args)` is a universal identity function.

steps.title: Create a scoped cache
steps.explanation: The cache is scoped to this memoized wrapper. Map supports an explicit membership check and avoids confusing a missing entry with a stored value of `undefined`.

steps.title: Define call equivalence explicitly
steps.explanation: The key selector defines which calls count as equivalent. Include every input that affects the result and keep the key's meaning stable for the cached function.

steps.title: Observe a cache hit
steps.explanation: The wrapped function executes on a cache miss, and its result is stored for later calls with the same key. This example uses a deterministic numeric calculation with both subtotal and rate in the key.

blocks.title: Memoization has correctness and memory costs
blocks.text: Do not cache a function whose output depends on hidden mutable state, time, locale or network state unless that dependency is part of the key or the cache has explicit invalidation. `JSON.stringify` is not universal: it fails on cycles and does not express object identity. A long-lived Map retains keys and results, so unbounded caching can cause memory growth. Caching async Promises also needs a policy for failures, stale data and expiration.

blocks.prompt: A memoized formatter uses `userId` as its cache key, but its output also depends on the active locale. What should change?

options.text: Include locale in the cache key or invalidate entries when locale changes
options.feedback: Every input that can change the output must participate in key selection or trigger invalidation, otherwise a different locale may reuse stale output.

options.text: Keep the key unchanged because Map automatically detects changed external state
options.feedback: Map compares the supplied keys; it does not observe external state or know what affects the result.

options.text: Use JSON.stringify on any possible input because it is an exact identity function
options.feedback: JSON serialization has edge cases and does not represent object identity or every possible input shape.

options.text: Replace memoization with debounce because it expires cache entries
options.feedback: Debounce controls when work starts after a burst of calls; it does not define a cache key or expiration policy.

blocks.explanation: A cache key is part of the function's correctness contract. Include all output-affecting inputs or invalidate entries when those inputs change.

blocks.title: Make the cache key match the function's real inputs
blocks.context: A UI formats monetary values using both amount and currency. A cache keyed only by amount can return a result formatted in the wrong currency.
instructions: Complete the memoized formatter so its key represents both amount and currency.
Call it twice with the same pair and explain why the second call can reuse the result.
Call it with the same amount and a different currency and show that the result is not reused incorrectly.
State which inputs would require invalidation if output also depended on locale or user preferences.
Explain how a long-lived cache could retain entries and name an appropriate bounded or invalidation strategy.
requirements: The key selector includes every input used by the output.
The formatter does not mutate input arguments.
A matching key may reuse a cached value, while a different currency yields a distinct key.
The explanation distinguishes memoization from debounce and HTTP caching.
The explanation covers cache lifetime or invalidation instead of claiming that memoization is always faster.
hints: The key selector should express call equivalence, not simply pick the first argument.
A cache is correct only if equal keys guarantee equivalent results or changes trigger invalidation.
For network data, consider in-flight request deduplication, caching successful results, errors and freshness separately.
successCriteria: The same amount/currency pair reuses a cached result.
The same amount in another currency does not receive a wrongly cached result.
The explanation identifies all output-affecting inputs in the key.
The design addresses cache growth or invalidation.
The solution distinguishes memoization from debounce and server/browser caching.

blocks.text: Add TTL and failure policy to async memoization

Memoization of async work has two states: an in-flight Promise can be shared by concurrent callers, while a successful result may be reused only until its freshness window expires. Start TTL after success, remove rejected entries so callers can retry, and guard settlement writes with entry identity so an invalidated older request cannot overwrite a newer entry. This example expires entries on lookup; TTL alone is not a hard memory cap, because untouched expired keys can remain in the Map. Use invalidation or an explicit size/eviction policy for high-cardinality keys.

steps.title: Validate the cache policy
steps.explanation: Reject invalid durations up front. The injected clock makes the example deterministic in tests without waiting for real wall-clock time.

steps.title: Share pending work and remove stale entries
steps.explanation: An entry with null expiry is still in-flight, so concurrent calls with the same key reuse its Promise. Expired entries are removed lazily when next requested.

steps.title: Set expiry after success and evict failures
steps.explanation: Expiry begins after success. A rejected Promise is removed to allow retry; checking that the Map still contains the same entry prevents an older completion from modifying the cache after invalidation or replacement.

steps.title: Expose invalidation and use a semantic key
steps.explanation: The key includes both user ID and locale because both can affect output. `invalidate` and `clear` expose explicit invalidation rather than assuming cached data remains correct forever.

blocks.prompt: Two callers request the same key while its network request is still pending. What should an async TTL cache do?

options.text: Start a second network request because no value has been cached yet
options.feedback: Without caching the in-flight Promise, concurrent callers duplicate work and may race to update the cache.

options.text: Share the in-flight Promise, start TTL after success, and remove the entry if it rejects
options.feedback: Promise sharing deduplicates in-flight work; success-based TTL provides a full freshness window, and rejection eviction permits retry.

options.text: Cache a rejected Promise until the TTL expires
options.feedback: Caching rejection can repeat a transient failure for every caller until expiry; this policy removes failed entries to permit retry.

options.text: Use JSON.stringify for every key because it preserves all identities
options.feedback: JSON serialization cannot represent every input or object identity; callers must still define semantic key equivalence.

blocks.explanation: An async cache should make in-flight, success, failure, expiration and invalidation policies explicit. A cached Promise is shared work, but a rejected result should not be treated as a successful value.

blocks.title: Build a deterministic async TTL cache
blocks.context: A profile panel fetches data by user ID and locale. Concurrent renders should share the in-flight request, successful data should expire after a freshness window, transient failures should be retryable, and invalidation must not be undone by an older request finishing later.
instructions: Implement `getOrLoad(key, loader)` so concurrent callers with the same key share one pending Promise.
Start TTL after the Promise fulfills; when a cached entry expires, discard it and load again.
If the loader rejects, remove that entry so a later call can retry instead of reusing a cached rejection.
Implement `invalidate(key)` and `clear()`; guard settlement handlers so an invalidated request cannot modify a newer cache entry.
Use an injected clock to test expiry boundaries without real timers, and explain why a TTL cache may need a max-size/eviction policy.
requirements: Concurrent requests for one semantic key share a single in-flight Promise.
The freshness window starts at successful completion rather than request start.
Rejected Promise entries are evicted so a later call can retry.
Invalidation during an in-flight request cannot let the old request overwrite or recreate its removed entry.
Tests cover before/at/after expiry deterministically with an injected clock.
The key includes every output-affecting input, including locale.
The explanation distinguishes TTL freshness from a hard memory-size limit.
hints: Use `expiresAt: null` for an entry whose Promise is pending; concurrent callers can share it.
Set `expiresAt = now() + ttlMs` only when the Promise resolves successfully.
On rejection, delete the entry only if the Map still points to that same entry object.
Invalidate should remove the mapping immediately; an older Promise resolving later must not repopulate or overwrite its removed entry.
TTL-on-access is lazy expiry, not a strict memory cap for keys never looked up again.
successCriteria: Same key + concurrent calls invoke the loader once and share the in-flight result.
A successful result is reused before expiry and refreshed at the expiry boundary.
A rejected load is removed and the next call can succeed.
Invalidation remains effective if a prior request settles afterward.
Tests are deterministic and do not sleep for wall-clock time.
The key covers user ID and locale, and the explanation describes cache growth.

blocks.title: Make a nested update without mutating the previous state
blocks.context: A UI keeps the previous state object for rendering, undo, or change detection. Mutating a nested object in place makes the old and new state share the same changed data.
instructions: Implement `updateCity(state, city)` so it returns a new state and a new `profile` object while leaving the input untouched.
Keep unrelated fields such as `preferences` shared unless your update changes them; explain why this is safe for an immutable update.
Add assertions showing that the original city remains unchanged, the returned city is updated, the outer and profile identities differ, and `preferences` retains identity.
Explain why `{ ...state }` alone would not be enough if you then mutate `next.profile.city`.
requirements: The function does not mutate the input state or its profile.
The returned outer object and changed profile have new identities.
Unchanged nested data remains equal and is not copied without reason.
Assertions cover both values and object identity.
hints: Copy the outer state and the nested profile; the other nested fields do not need copying for this change.
Use strict identity checks (`===` / `!==`) in addition to checking the displayed city.
A shallow copy is sufficient when you explicitly copy every container on the path you update.
successCriteria: before.profile.city is still 'Baku' and after.profile.city is 'Ganja'.
The explanation identifies the shared nested-reference bug in an outer-only spread.

steps.title: The returned methods close over local bindings
steps.explanation: The returned object methods can use count and largeCache after createCounter returns. The closure keeps those bindings reachable while the methods remain reachable.

steps.title: A reachable closure can retain more than you expect
steps.explanation: As long as counter remains reachable, its methods can use the captured values; the cache cannot be reclaimed just because the factory has returned.

steps.title: Dropping the last reference makes collection possible, not immediate
steps.explanation: If no other reference retains the object or captured environment, those objects become eligible for collection. JavaScript does not provide a general deterministic 'free now' command.

items: Detached DOM nodes kept in an array/listener may remain reachable even after removal from the visible page.
Listeners, subscriptions, timers and observers need lifecycle cleanup when they retain component-related objects.
An unbounded cache or closure over a large structure may be a design problem even when the garbage collector is working correctly.
Use heap snapshots and allocation timelines to investigate growth; a single high memory reading does not by itself prove a leak.

blocks.prompt: A function returns an object whose method closes over a local array. Why can the array remain allocated after the factory returns?

options.text: All local variables are kept forever
options.feedback: Locals may become unreachable; the runtime does not keep every local binding forever.

options.text: The returned method keeps the captured environment reachable
options.feedback: The method can still read the binding, so the captured environment and array remain reachable through the returned object.

options.text: Garbage collection only works for numbers
options.feedback: Garbage collection reclaims unreachable managed objects; the issue is reachability, not whether a value is numeric.

options.text: A closure copies all values into the call stack permanently
options.feedback: A closure keeps access to lexical bindings; it does not permanently freeze a copy of every captured value on the stack.

blocks.explanation: Reason about reachability from roots, not how long ago the function that created an object returned.

blocks.prompt: Which is the best first response to repeated 'Maximum call stack size exceeded' errors?

options.text: Find the repeating recursion/call cycle and establish a termination condition
options.feedback: A repeating call chain often reveals a missing base case or uncontrolled mutual recursion.

options.text: Assume the heap has run out of memory
options.feedback: This error usually signals stack exhaustion from too many nested calls, not a heap allocation failure.

options.text: Add setTimeout to every function without inspecting call flow
options.feedback: Scheduling work later may change execution timing but does not necessarily fix an infinite call cycle.

options.text: Remove every closure from the application
options.feedback: Closures are a normal language feature and are not the general cause of stack overflow.

blocks.explanation: Use the stack trace to identify a path of calls that fails to make progress.

blocks.title: Diagnose retained memory and runaway recursion
blocks.context: Write an evidence-based explanation rather than guessing from a memory graph or a single exception.
instructions: Trace the call stack for outer() → inner() and describe which call resumes after inner returns.
Repair a recursive function by stating its base case and the progress measure that reaches it.
Identify what references keep the object and captured array reachable in createCounter().
Propose a repeatable DevTools heap-snapshot/allocation-timeline investigation for an alleged leak.
Distinguish an object that is reachable by design from an object that is unintentionally retained.
requirements: The call-stack explanation follows last-in, first-out order.
The recursion fix guarantees progress toward a base case.
The memory explanation identifies concrete retaining references.
The investigation compares repeated scenarios and does not infer a leak from one snapshot alone.
hints: A recursive call must move toward a base case on every path.
A returned closure can retain its lexical environment.
For leak investigation, compare snapshots after repeatable actions and cleanup.
successCriteria: The recursion terminates for valid input.
The retaining reference is named correctly.
A repeatable memory investigation is described.
Reachable-by-design is distinguished from unintended retention.

items: Execution contexts model the active environment; the call stack records nested calls in LIFO order.
Objects remain while reachable; garbage collection timing is nondeterministic.
Closures can retain large structures, and leaks require evidence of unintended retention over time.
Engine-specific optimizations are implementation details, not portable language guarantees.
Memoization is valid only when the cache key represents all output-affecting inputs; long-lived caches need a retention and invalidation policy.
For async caches, share in-flight Promises, start TTL after success, evict failures, and guard invalidation races; TTL alone is not a hard size bound.
